passage.text: When firms first sent employees home in 2020, many managers predicted a collapse in output. The collapse never came. Studies covering tens of thousands of workers found that routine tasks were completed slightly faster at home, largely because commutes disappeared and meetings shrank. answer.text: Several cities have removed mature street trees to make room for extra lanes. The immediate gain is shorter queues at rush hour; the losses are less visible and last longer. The rational response is not to forbid road widening but to price what is being destroyed. Planners should publish the health and cooling benefits of a tree row beside the construction budget, and plant replacements before removal begins. When the trade-off is visible, citizens can judge whether a wider road is worth the shade it costs.

answer.text: The credibility of science rests on results that others can reproduce, yet large replication projects suggest that many published findings fail this test. The explanation is rarely fraud. Small samples, flexible analysis, and journals that reward novelty all push toward fragile results. Three reforms follow naturally. Researchers should register their analysis plan before collecting data, so that the reported model is not chosen after the fact. Journals should publish negative results, which currently disappear and force others to repeat the same dead ends. Funders should treat replication as ordinary research rather than as an admission of failure. None of these changes is dramatic, but together they restore the repetition on which science depends.

answer.text: Late-night revision feels productive because it is visible: the desk is occupied and the notes are open. Memory research suggests the feeling is misleading. During deep sleep the brain replays the patterns formed during the day and consolidates them, so a shortened night shortens the very process that turns study into recall. In controlled experiments, students who slept a full night remembered more than those who studied the same number of hours but slept half as long. The practical lesson is simple: review in the evening, sleep a full night, and test yourself in the morning. Schools can help by not scheduling early examinations immediately after late-night revision sessions.

passage.title: Carbon labels and the limits of consumer choice
passage.text: Carbon labels on products are attractive because they promise to turn every purchase into a climate decision. Trials in several countries show that labels do change behaviour, but modestly: shoppers shift a few percentage points toward lower-carbon options, and the effect fades when the label competes with price. The deeper problem is arithmetic. A label informs one choice at a time, while emissions are determined by systems: how food is produced, how goods are transported, how buildings are heated. Expecting labels to deliver large reductions is like expecting a menu to improve a restaurant's kitchen. Labels are worth having, but they work best alongside rules that change what is on offer.

items.stem: Write an essay of about 160 words on the following topic: some governments plan to require carbon labels on food and clothing. Discuss the benefits and limitations of this policy.

answer.text: Carbon labels promise to make climate impact visible at the moment of choice, and trials suggest they do shift purchases, if only by a few percentage points. That is a real gain: information is cheap and the label respects consumer judgement. Yet the policy has limits. Labels inform one decision at a time, while most emissions are fixed by production, transport and heating systems that no shopper can alter. The effect also fades when price pulls the other way, and poorer households can hardly be expected to pay more for a lower number. The sensible conclusion is to keep the label and pair it with rules that change what suppliers offer, so that the low-carbon option becomes the easy one.

answer.text: Platform work offers something salaried jobs rarely do: the freedom to choose when to work. It also transfers hidden costs to the worker. Independent contractors pay for their own insurance and retirement, and they absorb the cost of hours when no work arrives. Surveys that subtract these costs find hourly earnings below those of comparable salaried jobs. Banning platforms would remove the flexibility that workers say they value, so the better route is to separate the two issues. Platforms could contribute to a portable insurance account for every active hour, while workers keep control of their schedules. Flexibility would remain; the risk would be shared.
